name: Design a Full-Text Search Engine
intent: Find the few best documents for a free-text query among hundreds of millions, in tens of milliseconds, and keep the results fresh as the documents change.
codeTitle: an inverted index with BM25 and shards
finalIntro: One edited product becoming searchable, and one query with a typo finding it.
prompt: Design the search for an online store with 500 million product listings. Shoppers type a few words, possibly with a typo, and want the best 10 results in under 100 ms. Listings change all the time, and an edited price or title should appear in search within a few seconds. Support exact phrases, required and excluded words, and sorting that mixes relevance with how new a listing is.
functional: Search listings by free text, with words in any order
Support required words, excluded words and exact phrases
Rank the results by relevance, with the best first
Forgive typos and word endings, so 'wireles headphone' finds 'wireless headphones'
Show new and changed listings within a few seconds
Page through results and filter by fields such as category and price
nonFunctional: A query returns its top 10 in under 100 ms at the 99th percentile
Thousands of queries per second at the peak
An edit in the primary database is searchable within about 5 seconds
The search index is a derived copy: it can be lost and rebuilt, but never changes the source of truth
Survive the loss of a machine without losing search or documents
Grow by adding machines as the number of listings grows

firstAttempt.text: Keep the listings in a SQL table and search with a LIKE '%word%' condition on the title and description. For several words, add one condition per word. Order by the newest first.
limits: A leading wildcard cannot use an index, so every query reads every row of 500 million listings
There is no notion of relevance: a listing that mentions the word once ranks the same as one about nothing else
'Headphones' does not match 'headphone', and a typo matches nothing
Exact phrases and excluded words need slow extra conditions on the text
Search queries compete with orders and payments for the same database

steps.title: Analyze the text and build an inverted index
steps.problem: Scanning every listing for every query cannot work at 500 million listings, and plain text matching treats 'Headphones', 'headphone' and 'HEADPHONES' as different words.
steps.fix: Run every text through an analyzer: split it into words, lowercase them, drop very common stop words such as 'the' and 'of', and reduce each word to a stem, so 'running', 'runs' and 'run' share one term. Then build an inverted index, which is the index at the back of a book: for each term, a posting list of the sorted ids of the documents that contain it, with the position of each occurrence. A query is analyzed in the same way, and its terms are looked up in a dictionary. 'Red AND shoes' is the intersection of two sorted lists, done by walking them in step, starting with the shortest list and using skip pointers to jump over runs of the longer one. An exact phrase is an intersection followed by a check that the positions are consecutive.
steps.tradeoff: A query touches only the posting lists of its own terms, not the corpus, and the cost is about the length of the shortest list. The index takes disk space (typically the size of the text itself, once positions are stored), and the same analyzer must be used when indexing and when searching, or terms never meet. Stemming and stop words trade exactness for recall: a search for 'the who' needs special care.

steps.title: Write immutable segments and refresh them often
steps.problem: A compact, sorted, compressed posting list is slow to update in place, yet listings change constantly and a new listing should be searchable within seconds.
steps.fix: Never modify an index file. New documents are first collected in memory and written to a transaction log for durability. Every second or so a refresh turns the in-memory buffer into a new small immutable segment, which is a complete little inverted index, and from then on the documents are searchable. A query searches all segments and merges their answers. A delete only marks the document in a deleted-documents bitmap, and an update is a delete plus a new document. In the background, a merge policy combines small segments into larger ones, dropping the deleted documents for good.
steps.tradeoff: Writes are sequential and cheap, readers never take locks, and caches stay valid because a segment never changes. The cost is near-real-time rather than real-time search (there is a delay of about a refresh interval), several segments per query until merged, and merge work that uses disk and CPU and can compete with queries. Data is only durable once the log is flushed.

steps.title: Shard by document and answer by scatter-gather
steps.problem: 500 million listings and their index (about 2 TB) are too big for one machine, and one machine also limits the number of queries per second.
steps.fix: Split the documents over primary shards, each of 20 to 50 GB, by a hash of the document id. Each shard is a complete inverted index of its own documents, and each primary has replicas on other machines for fault tolerance and extra query capacity. A query goes to a coordinator, which sends it to one copy of every shard in parallel (scatter), lets each shard find its own top 10, and merges the shard lists into a global top 10 (gather). Choosing a replica per shard, for example the least busy one, spreads the load.
steps.tradeoff: Storage and indexing spread evenly, and capacity grows by adding shards and replicas. Every query now visits every shard, so the work per query grows with the number of shards, and the response time is that of the slowest shard, which makes the 99th percentile worse as shards are added. The number of primary shards is hard to change later, since the hash depends on it, so it is chosen with growth in mind.

steps.title: Rank with BM25 and stop early on the top 10
steps.problem: A query like 'red shoes' matches millions of listings, but only the best 10 matter, and sorting by date alone puts irrelevant new listings first.
steps.fix: Score each match with BM25, which rewards a term that is rare across the corpus (its inverse document frequency), counts more occurrences in the document with diminishing returns, and normalizes for document length so that a long text does not win by repetition. The score of a document is the sum over the query terms. Each shard keeps only a heap of its best 10 and, using the largest possible score of each block of postings, skips whole blocks that cannot enter the heap (block-max WAND). Collection statistics are made consistent across shards, or the scores will not be comparable. A freshness boost or a popularity factor is mixed into the final score by a function, for example by multiplying by a decay that halves every 30 days.
steps.tradeoff: Results are ordered by usefulness and the cost depends on the top 10, not on the number of matches. Scores are relative, tuned by hand and judged by experiments, because relevance has no single correct answer. A strong freshness boost makes new but weak listings beat better old ones, and the total number of hits becomes approximate once early termination is on.

steps.title: Forgive typos with edit distance and n-grams
steps.problem: Shoppers misspell words, and a term that is not in the dictionary returns nothing, even when the right listing exists.
steps.fix: For each query term, find dictionary terms within one or two edits (insert, delete, replace or swap a letter) using a finite-state automaton run over the sorted term dictionary, which touches only a tiny part of it. Matches at a smaller distance score higher, and the first letters must match exactly to bound the cost. Another option is to index every term as character n-grams (for example 'wir', 'ire', 'rel') and find terms that share many n-grams. Both methods are used to suggest 'did you mean' and to expand the query.
steps.tradeoff: Misspelled queries find the right listings and the search feels forgiving. Fuzzy expansion multiplies the number of posting lists to read, so it is limited to terms of enough length and to a few expansions, and it can add wrong matches, such as 'sale' for 'sole'. Exact matches must still rank above fuzzy ones.

steps.title: Feed the index from the primary database through change events
steps.problem: The search index is a copy, and writing to it from the application on every change leads to missed updates, double work, and an index that quietly drifts away from the database.
steps.fix: The primary database stays the source of truth. Every change is written, in the same transaction, to an outbox table (or read from the database's replication log by change data capture) and published as an event with the document id and a version. An indexer consumes the events in order per document, reads the current row, analyzes it and sends it to the right shard with the version as the document version, so an old event never overwrites a newer one. To change the analyzer or the mapping, build a new index from a full scan, keep it in step with the event log, and then switch an alias to it.
steps.tradeoff: The index follows the database within seconds without the application knowing about search, and it can be rebuilt at any time. Search is eventually consistent: a listing that has just been deleted may still appear for a few seconds, so the result page must check the status when it matters. Rebuilding a very large index takes hours and needs spare capacity.

failures.scenario: One shard is slow or its machine is lost during a query
failures.impact: The coordinator is waiting for the last answer, so the whole query is slow, or the query returns without that shard's documents.
failures.answer: Each shard has replicas, so the coordinator retries on another copy, or sends the request to two copies and uses the first answer. A deadline lets it return partial results from the shards that answered, marked as partial, rather than nothing. A replica is promoted to primary when a primary is lost, and a new replica is rebuilt by copying segments.

failures.scenario: A huge merge or a burst of indexing slows queries down
failures.impact: Disk and CPU are used by merges and by the indexing of a bulk load, and query latency rises for everyone.
failures.answer: Merges are throttled, indexing is rate limited and queued, and a bulk load disables the refresh until it ends. Heavy indexing runs on separate nodes or in off-peak hours, and the number of segments per shard is watched as a signal.

failures.scenario: The index falls behind or disagrees with the database
failures.impact: Edited prices show old values and deleted listings still appear.
failures.answer: Lag of the change event log is alerted on. Events carry the document version, so replays and duplicates are harmless. A periodic job compares counts and checksums with the database and repairs differences, and a full rebuild into a new index followed by an alias switch fixes anything else. Pages show the current price from the database, not from search.

failures.scenario: One very expensive query, such as a leading wildcard or a very deep page
failures.impact: The query reads huge amounts of data on every shard, and the node runs out of memory or time.
failures.answer: Limits on query cost: no leading wildcards, a maximum number of fuzzy expansions, a maximum page depth (use a cursor over the sort values beyond it), and a timeout per shard. Circuit breakers on memory stop a query before it takes down a node.

alternatives.title: How to split the index

options.name: By document (each shard is a full index of some documents)
options.pro: Even load, simple writes, and every shard can score on its own

options.name: By term (each shard holds some terms' posting lists)
options.pro: A query only visits the shards of its terms
options.con: Long lists have to be shipped between machines to intersect, and popular terms make hot spots

alternatives.pick: By document. Splitting by term moves more data over the network, which costs more than the extra shard visits.

alternatives.title: How to score

options.name: TF-IDF
options.con: Term frequency has no limit, so repeating a word wins, and length is handled crudely

options.name: BM25
options.pro: Saturating term frequency and length normalization, a strong default
options.con: Has parameters, and still knows nothing about meaning or popularity

options.name: BM25 then a learned re-ranker on the top 100
options.pro: Uses clicks, freshness and meaning for a better order
options.con: Needs training data, more machines and more latency

alternatives.pick: BM25 to find candidates, with a freshness factor, and a learned re-ranker later if the metrics justify it.

alternatives.title: How to handle typos

options.name: Edit-distance automaton over the term dictionary
options.pro: Exact distance control and no extra index
options.con: Costly for short terms or large distances

options.name: Character n-gram index
options.pro: Fast candidate lookup and also helps with partial words
options.con: A bigger index and more false candidates

options.name: Spelling suggestions from query logs
options.pro: Corrects to what people really type
options.con: Needs a lot of traffic and fails for rare words

alternatives.pick: Edit distance of 1 (or 2 for long words) at query time, with query-log suggestions for the most common mistakes.

alternatives.title: How to feed the index

options.name: The application writes to both
options.con: A failure between the two writes leaves them different, and nothing repairs it

options.name: Outbox or change data capture, then an indexer
options.pro: No lost updates, replayable, and the app is unaware of search
options.con: Another pipeline to run, and the lag must be watched

options.name: Periodic full re-index
options.con: Hours of delay and heavy load on the database

alternatives.pick: Change events for freshness, with a periodic full reconciliation as a safety net.

quiz.question: An online store with 500 million listings finds products with LIKE '%word%' on the title. Searches take many seconds, 'headphone' does not match 'headphones', and every query reads every row. What is the best change?
options: Analyze text into stemmed terms and build an inverted index of sorted posting lists to intersect
Add a B-tree index on the title and description columns so the database can look up the rows containing each word
Split the table into 50 shards by listing id and run the LIKE query on all shards in parallel, dividing the scan time
Precompute the results of the 10,000 most common searches and store them in a lookup table for instant answers
quiz.explanation: An inverted index touches only the posting lists of the query's terms, and stemming makes related word forms meet. A B-tree cannot be used for a leading wildcard, so it still scans every row. Sharding the scan divides the cost but keeps it linear, and precomputed answers cover only the common queries.

quiz.question: The index of 500 million listings is about 2 TB, and a query is sent to every primary shard, with the coordinator waiting for the slowest. The team can choose a shard size of roughly 5 GB, 35 GB or 250 GB, and the shard count is hard to change later. Which choice is best?
options: About 400 shards of roughly 5 GB, because smaller shards search faster and more parallel work lowers latency
About 60 shards of roughly 35 GB, since per-query work and tail latency grow with the shard count and the count is fixed by the hash
About 8 shards of roughly 250 GB, to minimise the fan-out, with replicas added whenever more capacity is needed
About 60 shards split by term range, so each query visits only the shards that hold the posting lists of its terms
quiz.explanation: Around 20 to 50 GB per shard balances fan-out against shard size. With 400 shards every query contacts 400 machines and the p99 is set by the slowest of them. 250 GB shards make recovery and merges heavy, and splitting by term ships long posting lists across the network.

quiz.question: An indexer reads change events for listing 42. It indexes version 8 (listing removed) and then, because of a redelivery, receives the older version 7 (price changed). The removed listing now appears in search again. What is the right fix?
options: Process events by the time the indexer receives them so that the latest arrival always wins
Turn off redelivery in the indexer so an old event can never come back after a newer one
Carry the row version from the database as the document version, so the index rejects any write with a lower version
Shorten the refresh interval to 100 ms so that the newer state becomes visible before the old redelivered event is applied
quiz.explanation: A version carried from the source of truth makes duplicates and reordering harmless, because an old event cannot overwrite a newer one. Arrival time is exactly what a redelivery breaks. Turning off redelivery loses updates after any failure, and a faster refresh only changes when data becomes visible, not which version wins.
